headline: Land market downturn recovery now pushed to mid-to-late 2027, with further rate hikes risking additional delay of one to two quarters
reasoning: Matt Bell indicates that the expected end of the housing land market downturn, previously forecast for late 2025 or early 2026, has shifted to mid-2027. He notes that in housing markets, rate rises flow through faster than the broader economy — around 6 to 9 months versus 12 to 18 months — meaning any September rate hike would push recovery out by another quarter or two. He also flags that if two further rate hikes occur, the downturn would extend even further.
quote: We would have thought that the downturn probably would have been ending closer to the end of this year and some recovery being seen in the first quarter of 2027, calendar 2027. That's probably shifted out now to closer to the second half or the middle of the year. Um, so it absolutely is having an effect. And as you know, if there were two more rate hikes that would push out even further. We talked about 12 to 18 months for rate rises to flow through to the economy a bit quicker. In housing markets it's more like 6 to 9 months. So another rate hike in September really pushes that out, you know another quarter or six months.
episode_title: The land market's tale of two Australias

headline: Cutting migration would lower demand and price growth, particularly in Adelaide, but is a short-term fix to a long-term problem; fixing housing supply is preferable
reasoning: Matt Bell explains that some markets, such as Adelaide, are almost entirely dependent on net overseas migration for population growth, as net interstate migration is roughly zero and natural increases are offset. Reducing migration would therefore directly lower housing demand and dampen price growth. He is critical of using migration as an easy lever because significant economic and social benefits are lost; he prefers addressing the underlying housing supply and affordability issues directly.
quote: Undoubtedly it impacts markets. I mean, some of our markets like Adelaide, you know, their net interest or sorry, their overall migration is nearly completely dependent on net overseas migration with sort of net negative net interstate migration, sort of, um, you know, zeroing out the natural increases. So some markets really are dependent on it and it will lower demand. And just like it will and the established market will lower price growth. Um, I'm not a massive fan of trying to drive a short term fix to a long term problem. I would rather us just fix housing supply and housing issues rather than jump to the easy lever of migration where you lose a significant amount of benefits as well.
episode_title: The land market's tale of two Australias

headline: Three rate hikes in H1 have driven three quarters of easing in capital city land markets, with sales volumes hit hardest in Melbourne and Sydney while Perth and Queensland remain hot
reasoning: Matt Bell explains that the primary driver of weakness in the land market is interest rate hikes, with three hikes in the first half flowing through to sentiment, borrowing capacity and demand. Melbourne and Sydney are operating well below long-term sales volume trends, while prices have been more stable than volumes. Perth and south-east Queensland remain strong markets, with Perth still seeing 17% price growth, though they too have eased somewhat. Supply constraints in south-east Queensland mean that market could be selling more lots if supply were available.
quote: Same as all property markets at the moment. It's primarily rates. Obviously there is impact and secondary impacts from the budget changes for investor taxation. But really you know we're feeling the effects of three rate hikes in the first half. You know already in the June quarter which these numbers you know are tracking. And really it has been since the rate outlook changed in November, December and 25 that we saw that that change in activity.
episode_title: The land market's tale of two Australias

headline: Underlying housing demand remains structurally intact, driven by population growth and household formation independent of rate cycle
reasoning: Bell distinguishes between cyclical demand (which is rate-sensitive) and underlying demand, which he ties to population growth and household formation. He argues that underlying demand for new housing remains strong regardless of the rate environment. Volumes are the leading indicator in land markets, and prices typically follow volumes with a lag on both the upside and downside.
quote: When we talk about underlying housing demand, it really is outside rates to be honest. We're talking about population growth driving that. You know, households being formed. Um, and and just, you know, that demand for new housing that more people drives.
episode_title: The land market's tale of two Australias

reasoning: Bell does not expect a generational downturn, characterising the current cycle as a 'pretty standard downturn.' He had previously expected recovery to begin around end-2026 and early 2027, but the July inflation print has pushed his outlook for recovery to the middle or second half of 2027. Each additional rate hike extends the downturn by roughly a quarter to six months, given housing markets transmit rate rises over 6-9 months. He sees the federal budget's investor tax changes as marginally shifting investors from established markets into new land markets, which retain negative gearing and CGT concessions.
quote: We would have thought that I think that the downturn probably would have been ending closer to the end of this year and some recovery being seen in the first quarter of 2027, calendar 2027. That's probably shifted out now to closer to the second half or the middle of the year. Um, so it absolutely is having an effect. And as you know, if there were two more rate write rate hikes that would push out even further. We talked about, you know, we talk about 12 to 18 months for rate rises to to flow through to the economy a bit quicker. In housing markets it's more like 6 to 9 months. So another rate hike in September really pushes that out, you know another quarter or six months.

headline: Matt Bell flags strong household spending and low unemployment as upside inflation risks that could support further RBA hikes
reasoning: Bell points to annual household spending growth running at around 6% against population growth of only 1.5% as a significant upside risk to the inflation outlook. He also notes the unemployment rate remaining low as a further data point supporting the case for additional hikes. He acknowledges these metrics are more influential for the RBA than house price weakness, making the risk of further hikes non-trivial despite his base case of a long hold.
quote: You know, annual increases in monthly household spending has, has been trending up pretty clearly. It's sitting at 6%. If you've got population at 1.5%, then that I guess poses upside risks for for that inflation outlook. Um, you know, even the unemployment rate staying low. I know the RBA upped their forecasts of of it softening I guess. But but those two elements are the, I guess the data points that support the view that there could be more hikes coming. Um, and that, you know, they're more important than what any weakness we might be seeing in, in the, um, you know, in house prices.

headline: Matt Bell (Oliver Hume) sees Australian rates at peak with next move likely down, but extended hold period expected
reasoning: Bell interprets the RBA's updated forecasts, which show underlying inflation returning to the middle of the target band within 18 months at the current 4.35% cash rate, as signal that rates are at their peak. Despite the governor's hawkish tone around upside external risks (global conflict, supply shocks), Bell places more weight on the statement's forecasts than on the governor's rhetoric. He believes if no major external shocks materialise, the next rate move will be downward. He expects a long hold period before any cuts eventuate.
quote: I put a lot more. I guess I put some more weight in in the actual forecast coming out in the statement, which, you know, have underlying inflation returning to the middle of the target band within 18 months, which is the shortest time frame we've had for a long time in terms of getting back there, you know. And that is with, um, you know, the market forecast or the cash rate staying where it is at 4.35%. So I guess on balance, I think I understand why the government, why the government has said it, there are more potential for upside external surprises when it comes to inflation, external environment, global war, all that sort of stuff. But clearly the Bank has made the call that at the current settings, they're restrictive. And if there's no big external shocks, then we will be getting that underlying inflation back to target in, uh, you know, in 18 months. And we should be expecting the next move to be down if that is the case.

headline: Matt Bell argues the negative wealth effect from falling house prices is real but property declines remain a 'blip' in long-term context
reasoning: Bell acknowledges the governor's comments that house prices are not the RBA's primary concern except insofar as they flow through to consumer wealth and spending. He agrees a negative wealth effect from declining house prices can act similarly to a rate hike. However, he contextualises current declines as modest in long-term chart terms, noting even a 5-10% correction across major capitals would barely register historically.
quote: Yeah. It does. I mean, the governor was pretty unequivocal yesterday when she mentioned, you know, that house prices are not the main game except as to your point how it flows through via the wealth effects... And if you put it in the long term context, as I think the governor referred to, you, look at those charts of of house prices across all those major capitals, it's a blip. Even if we get to 5 to 10% across some.

headline: Expects existing property investors to hold but a large cohort of new investors to exit established market, with some shifting to new builds and apartments
reasoning: Matt Bell argues that existing investors have no incentive to sell because holding preserves access to the more favourable CGT and negative gearing tax treatment. However, each year approximately 150,000 new investors enter the established property market, and a material proportion of these will now redirect capital into equities, other asset classes, or new residential developments where CGT and negative gearing advantages are retained. This shift is a short-term exacerbating factor for established property prices, though still dwarfed by the 20-30% gains most markets have seen over the past couple of years. Treasury's own forecast of a 2-5% decline over one to two years remains the central case.
quote: I think there's no incentive to sell. I mean, you know, if you're an investor that's in the market, you're incentivized to hold to keep the more attractive CGT and negative gearing, you know, tax regime there. So there's but, you know, every year there is 150,000 new property investors into the established market. Some proportion of those a large proportion of those will not not go there anymore. You know, they will just either go into equities or some other investment class, or they will shift into the new market where you do retain those negative gearing and capital gains advantages. So that won't be, you know, the majority of them, but there will be some proportion that will shift into into new markets and apartments, new house and land. But there absolutely is a large cohort that is no longer going to be investing in property. Hence it's exacerbating in the short term.

headline: Matt Bell sees ANZ's bearish housing forecasts as overdone, expects moderate downturn with recovery in 2027
reasoning: Matt Bell believes ANZ's forecast of up to 15% peak-to-trough decline in Sydney and 10% in Melbourne is on the bearish side. He notes the current rate hiking cycle is only 75 basis points in housing-downturn terms, which is small by historical standards. He expects a weak end to 2026 followed by a recovery in 2027, supported by ongoing strong population growth and persistent housing undersupply evidenced by still-rising rents. Budget taxation changes on property are seen as a modest exacerbating factor rather than the primary driver. He firmly rejects the idea of a decade-long housing price correction.
quote: I think if we when we get to it, the housing downturn will have been exacerbated slightly by the budget taxation changes. But mainly it's driven by by the rates changes. And it's really you know, it's really only 75 basis points of increases. That's small in terms of historical context of of, you know, rate hike, hiking cycles that have driven a housing downturn. So I tend to be on the side that, you know, we'll we'll have a week end of 26, um, at about 27 will be a recovery. So I tend to think that, um, the ANZ numbers are a little bit higher than what I would expect. Um, certainly in international sense. Um, and I suspect that, you know, the drivers that we know that are underlying the market, the the continued strong population growth, we've still got a housing undersupply. And we know that because things like rents are still rising, etcetera, etcetera. So, you know, that might be a bit overdone.

headline: Matt Bell sees June and September quarters as toughest for Australian property market, but expects recovery signals by December and uptick by Q1 2027
reasoning: Bell expects the next six months to be challenging for both established and new dwelling markets, with weak price growth, low volumes, elevated listings, and subdued auction clearance rates. However, he notes some indicators have already begun to recover off their lows — Melbourne clearance rates recovering from below 50% to around 60%, and consumer sentiment measures ticking up. He argues that actual rate cuts are not necessary to restart property market growth; consumer confidence that hikes are finished will be sufficient. He anticipates sustainably positive but lower-than-historical growth once investors return, and expects a geographic divergence with Sydney and Melbourne underperforming Brisbane, Perth, and Adelaide.
quote: I think the next six months will be will be tough. You know, I think probably the June and September quarters will be the toughest, both in terms of the established market. And, you know, that obviously flows through to the new dwelling market as well. Uh, you know, we're still seeing weak results. We're still seeing, um, you know, weak price growth volumes. Um, higher listings, uh, pretty low auction rates. But some of those numbers have already come off the bottom. I mean, Melbourne hit 60%, which is still low, but it's not below 50% where it was. We're seeing some of the consumer sentiment measures come off the bottom... I think we're probably going to have, um, September being in line with where we see June. I wouldn't be surprised if we saw some positive indications by December... I am expecting to see, you know, uptick, certainly by the first quarter of 2027, in both established and and new land markets.
